title: Riesgo en Nvidia, justicia intoxicada por IA y satélites que llevan centros de datos al espacio
script:
Bienvenidos a Radio IA, hoy es 26 de noviembre de 2026. Les traemos varias historias sobre cómo la inteligencia artificial está tensando las finanzas, los tribunales, la regulación y hasta la infraestructura física del planeta.

Empezamos con Nvidia. La agencia S&P Global Ratings está considerando rebajar la calificación crediticia de la compañía, citando preocupaciones sobre su gestión y sus prácticas de gobierno corporativo. Según TechCrunch, a pesar del sólido desempeño financiero de Nvidia, la salida y posterior reincorporación del consejero delegado Jensen Huang ha levantado dudas sobre lo que S&P llama “supervisión ejecutiva débil y falta de planificación de sucesión”, además de un “riesgo de persona clave” por la fuerte dependencia de Huang. La agencia espera terminar su revisión en 90 días y podría recortar la nota de AA a AA-. Mi lectura es que esto va mucho más allá del prestigio corporativo: aunque Nvidia mantendría el grado de inversión, una rebaja encarecería su deuda y, como Nvidia respalda a neoclouds y otras empresas de infraestructura que no tienen crédito sólido por sí solas, esa deuda ajena también podría volverse más cara o exigir más garantías. Esto sugiere que la gobernanza se está convirtiendo en un costo financiero directo para el ecosistema de infraestructura de IA.

Pasamos a los tribunales de Inglaterra y Gales. Una investigación del Bureau of Investigative Journalism compartida con The Guardian ha encontrado que el uso no declarado de IA ha afectado a más de dos docenas de casos judiciales este año. Según The Guardian, los jueces se han quejado de declaraciones de testigos generadas por IA, jurisprudencia ficticia y estatutos inexistentes. En un caso, un agente de policía usó IA para redactar una declaración de una víctima con la instrucción de lograr “la sentencia más alta y la declaración más lacrimógena para hacer llorar a un juez o lector”. En otro, un abogado citó una sentencia inventada por una IA alucinando. Brett Dixon, presidente del Law Society, dijo que los documentos generados por IA están consumiendo más tiempo de los jueces y socavando los esfuerzos por reducir el atraso judicial. Mi lectura es que esto introduce un nuevo costo económico oculto en el sistema legal: cada minuto judicial dedicado a revisar material fabricado es tiempo que no se usa para resolver casos reales, y cada advertencia de los jueces revela una vulnerabilidad que antes no existía a esta escala. Esto sugiere que la productividad prometida por la IA en despachos y comisarías puede estar generando justo lo contrario en la fase más cara del sistema.

Ahora, el choque entre Meta y el regulador financiero británico. Según Wired, la Autoridad de Conducta Financiera del Reino Unido se ha quejado de que Meta se negó a compartir su agente personal Muse para realizar pruebas conjuntas antes de su lanzamiento en el país. Colin Payne, jefe de innovación del regulador, dijo que “es otra fuerza de ataque, agentes saliendo a la calle, la mayoría viniendo de Estados Unidos”. La FCA quería investigar cómo serían las interacciones entre Muse y un cliente normal, especialmente cómo se harán los pagos cuando los agentes actúan de forma autónoma. Meta dice que ha colaborado de forma constructiva con las autoridades, pero solo avisó a la FCA de sus planes el mes pasado. Mi lectura es que este desencuentro refleja una asimetría de poder creciente: las plataformas pueden desplegar agentes a escala masiva más rápido de lo que los supervisores pueden examinarlos. Esto sugiere que la supervisión financiera se está convirtiendo en una carrera contra el calendario, no solo contra la tecnología.

Miremos ahora a América Latina. Según CNBC, el cobre, el petróleo, el gas y las tierras raras de la región podrían beneficiarse de la creciente demanda energética de la IA, pero la infraestructura y la política fiscal son la verdadera prueba. Chile tiene cobre, Argentina está ampliando sus exportaciones de petróleo y gas, y Brasil tiene una matriz eléctrica renovable y grandes reservas de tierras raras. La producción de cobre de Chile cayó un 8,5% en los primeros nueve meses de 2026, mientras la demanda de cobre refinado crecerá un 1,6% este año y un 2% el próximo. Goldman Sachs prevé que la demanda eléctrica de los centros de datos crecerá un 170% para 2030. Mi lectura es que el cuello de botella no está bajo tierra, sino en la capacidad de refinar, transportar y financiar proyectos con reglas estables. Rafael Ch, de Signum Global Advisors, lo resume: un productor en Vaca Muerta puede tener pozos excelentes y aun así no poder exportar sin capacidad de oleoductos y acceso a puertos. Esto sugiere que los ganadores no serán solo los dueños de los recursos, sino los países capaces de convertir esos recursos en proyectos viables para inversores impacientes.

Volvemos al software. OpenAI ha comenzado a unificar las experiencias de Chat y Work en ChatGPT, según TechCrunch. Un portavoz dijo que la mayoría de los usuarios no verá restricciones más frecuentes, pero una pequeña fracción de los usuarios más intensivos podría alcanzar sus límites antes. Bajo el nuevo sistema, Chat y Work compartirán un solo medidor de uso, aunque las conversaciones con el modelo Instant seguirán siendo ilimitadas. La preocupación de algunos suscriptores es pagar lo mismo por menos acceso a los modelos de razonamiento avanzado. Mi lectura es que esto es una señal clara de la presión de costos de inferencia: las compañías de IA están racionando silenciosamente el acceso de los clientes más costosos de servir. Esto sugiere que la era de la generosidad de los chatbots está terminando, y que la rentabilidad por suscriptor empieza a importar más que el crecimiento bruto de uso.

Y cerramos con una historia que parece de ciencia ficción. Según The Verge, la Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones de Estados Unidos autorizó a SpaceX a desplegar hasta 1 millón de satélites equipados con chips de IA como parte de su iniciativa Starmind. La aprobación exige desplegar al menos un satélite para 2033 y cumplir el hito de 1 millón para 2040. SpaceX describe el proyecto como una forma de capturar energía solar en el espacio para alimentar capacidades de IA en la Tierra, transmitiendo datos mediante láseres de alta velocidad conectados a Starlink. Google ya ha lanzado un satélite de su proyecto Suncatcher, y Blue Origin hará el primer lanzamiento pesado dedicado para ese proyecto en 2029. Mi lectura es que el espacio se está convirtiendo en la nueva frontera de la capacidad de cómputo, empujada por los límites energéticos y térmicos de los centros de datos terrestres. Esto sugiere que la infraestructura de la IA empieza a buscar soluciones cada vez más extremas, con plazos de una década o más, mientras la demanda crece trimestre a trimestre.

Qué mirar mañana. Estaremos atentos a si S&P confirma o descarta la rebaja de Nvidia, a cualquier reacción del regulador británico sobre Muse, y si aparecen nuevos casos judiciales afectados por IA no declarada. También conviene seguir las señales de precios del cobre y de inversión en infraestructura latinoamericana, porque ahí se está jugando el suministro físico de la próxima ola de centros de datos.

stories.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
stories.summary: The credit rating agency may lower Nvidia's credit rating to AA-, the fourth-highest rating.
stories.body:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.
In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

stories.title: Dozens of court cases in England and Wales affected by undisclosed AI use in 2026
stories.summary:
Exclusive: Investigation finds at least 25 cases affected by AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes

Undisclosed AI use has affected more than two dozen court cases this year, prompting judges to complain about AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, an investigation has revealed.

Proceedings where judges have been forced to deal with lawyers, police officers and claimants misusing the technology in 2026 include a high court dispute between tax lawyers marred by what the judge called “unacceptable” use of “generative AI hallucinations” and references to nonexistent cases.

stories.body:
Undisclosed AI use has affected more than two dozen court cases this year, prompting judges to complain about AI-generated witness statements, fictitious case law and nonexistent statutes, an investigation has revealed.
Proceedings where judges have been forced to deal with lawyers, police officers and claimants misusing the technology in 2026 include a high court dispute between tax lawyers marred by what the judge called “unacceptable” use of “generative AI hallucinations” and references to nonexistent cases.
Another involved a police officer in a grievous bodily harm case who used AI to write a witness statement so it would maximise the attacker’s sentence and “make a judge … weep”. A barrister in a $21m (£16m) high court dispute between two Nigerian oil companies made an argument based on a ruling – supposedly by a senior judge – that had been entirely invented by a hallucinating AI, leading the judge to warn of “the dangers of relying on the product of AI without verification”.
The spate of cases in which problems with AI tools have occurred in 2026 – at least 25, according to a trawl of published judgments by the Bureau of Investigative Journalism shared with the Guardian – comes despite a series of warnings from senior legal figures about the danger of the technology when used to cut corners and build cases. Brett Dixon, the president of the Law Society, told the Guardian AIs producing verbose case documents, particularly when non-lawyers represent themselves, is also taking up more of judges’ time, undermining efforts to clear court backlogs.
“You go from three pages from a lawyer … using human judgment to a rambling 60 pages from a commercial AI,” he said.
Last week, the supreme court judge Lord Sales also said the supreme court was growing “increasingly concerned” about AI and highlighted fears the technology could leave the legal profession deskilled.
“The danger is not simply that the machine gets the answer wrong,” he said. “The greater long-term danger is that human beings gradually lose the ability to know whether it has got the answer wrong.”
Cases affected by AI this year often involved people representing themselves, but also legal professionals increasingly using the technology to accelerate research, save time and increase earnings. Earlier this month the problem hit the Crown Prosecution Service when one of its lawyers cited an imaginary legal precedent.
Among the cases so far in 2026 a senior insolvency judge, Mark Mullen, discovered a junior solicitor had relied on an AI chatbot to research a point of law and took its invented quote from a fictitious statute. The judge examined the AI chat logs and discovered it had produced “nonsense” and warned in his judgment “AI has the potential to be wholly unreliable”.
In another case, the court of appeal dismissed an application for a convicted criminal from Derbyshire to challenge a four-year prison sentence for crimes including grievous bodily harm. The man had pleaded guilty after smashing his way through a glass patio door with a shovel to get into a house where the mother of his children had barricaded herself with a friend and her child. He threatened them with a large kitchen knife, fled and in the process broke a police officer’s shoulder.
The investigating police officer created a victim personal statement (VPS) by uploading a transcript of the mother’s interviews to Microsoft’s Copilot AI and prompting it “to achieve the highest sentence and the most tear-jerking VPS to make a judge or reader weep when reading”.
After the officer was removed from frontline duty the appeal court judges warned that “that no police officer should ever prepare a witness statement of any kind in this way”.

stories.title: Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains
stories.summary: The FCA warned against “another force of attack” from agents after the company declined a request to work on joint testing ahead of rolling out its personal agent in the UK on Tuesday.
stories.body:
Meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.
“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), said Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.
His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.
The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys said they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he says.
Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month.
“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.
More than 10 million users have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne says.
The ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.
“If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA said in a statement.

stories.title: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test
stories.summary: Latin America’s copper, oil, gas and rare earths could benefit from rising AI energy demand, if infrastructure and fiscal policy attract investment.
stories.body:
Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.
But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.
"We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added.
Ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. "We are currently neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months," he said.
Where the investment case is strongest
The investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves.
Chile's copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply.
But demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group. Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids.
Chile's copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships.
Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. "As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose," he said.
The scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how quickly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.
Turning resources into investment
The investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA.
"Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand," said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
"But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value," she added.
Some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029.
Argentina shows the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets.
"I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports.
That gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production," Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina's vast shale basin.

stories.title: OpenAI says heavy ChatGPT users may hit limits sooner as it merges Chat and Work
stories.summary: OpenAI will introduce a single usage meter across ChatGPT as it combines the Chat and Work experiences.
stories.body:
OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.
The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.
That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees.
Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.
While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.
Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.
The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

stories.title: FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
stories.summary: In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company's "Starmind" initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency […]
stories.body:
In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.
FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.
The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.
SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.
Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.
